front: PThreads: what does the name stand for, and what does POSIX describe?
back: PThreads = POSIX Threads, the de facto threading standard on UNIX systems. POSIX (Portable Operating System Interface) describes the system call interface that OSes need to support, to increase interoperability among OSes. Within POSIX, PThreads describes the threading API for creating, using and managing threads, including synchronization constructs such as mutexes and condition variables.

front: PThreads: what data type represents a thread, and what does it hold?
back: pthread_t. It holds the thread's identifier, its execution state, and other thread-relevant information. Most of this is not seen directly by developers; it is used and maintained by the pthreads library.

front: PThreads: give the full signature of pthread_create.
back: int pthread_create(pthread_t *thread, const pthread_attr_t *attr, void * (*start_routine)(void *), void *arg);

front: pthread_create: what does its return value mean?
back: It returns an int indicating whether the creation was a success or a failure.

front: PThreads: give the full signature of pthread_join and what each argument is.
back: int pthread_join(pthread_t thread, void **status); The first argument is the thread to be joined; status captures all the relevant return information, as well as the results returned by that thread. It returns an int indicating success or failure.

front: PThreads vs Birrell: which pthreads constructs correspond to Birrell's Thread, Fork and Join, and how do the pthread_create arguments map to Fork's?
back:
• Thread: pthread_t
  • Fork: pthread_create; start_routine is Fork's proc, arg is Fork's arguments
  • Join: pthread_join

front: PThreads: what features of a new thread can the pthread_attr_t structure define?
back:
• stack size
  • scheduling policy
  • priority
  • system/process scope
  • inheritance
  • joinable

front: pthread_create: what happens if you pass NULL in place of a pthread_attr_t?
back: PThreads falls back to default behavior for the new thread.

front: PThreads: what do pthread_attr_init and pthread_attr_destroy do?
back: pthread_attr_init allocates space for a pthread_attr_t and sets its fields to the pthreads default values; pthread_attr_destroy deallocates that space.

front: PThreads: how do you read and modify individual fields of a pthread_attr_t?
back: With the pthread_attr_{set/get}{attribute} family of calls.

front: PThreads vs Birrell: which thread mechanism in pthreads was not considered by Birrell?
back: Detachable threads. The pthreads default, joinable threads, matches what Birrell described.

front: PThreads: what is the default joinability of a newly created thread, and what must the parent do?
back: The default is joinable. For a joinable child, the parent should not terminate until the child has completed and been joined with an explicit join. If the parent exits early, the children may become zombies: completed or dead, but never exited or reaped properly.

front: PThreads: what is a detached thread, and what does detaching make the parent/child relationship become?
back: A detached thread cannot be joined back into the parent, so the parent may exit early while the children keep running. Detaching makes parent and children equivalent, except the parent still holds some extra information about the children it created.

front: PThreads: give the two ways to detach a thread.
back:
• Call int pthread_detach(pthread_t thread);
  • Set pthread_attr_setdetachstate(attr, PTHREAD_CREATE_DETACHED); on the attributes, then pass attr to pthread_create.

front: PThreads: once children are detached, how can the parent thread finish?
back: It does not need to wait for the children, so it can simply exit with pthread_exit.

front: PThreads: in the custom-options creation example, what two attributes are adjusted on the new thread, and in what order are the steps done?
back: The attribute structure is created and initialized first (allocating memory and setting pthreads defaults). Then the detach state is set to PTHREAD_CREATE_DETACHED and the scheduling scope to system scope (so the thread shares resources equally with all threads in the system). The structure is then passed to pthread_create.

front: Join: lecture says undetached pthreads must be joined or they become zombies. What does Birrell say about Join?
back: Join is not called very much at SRC, some thread facilities do not provide it at all, and a thread whose procedure returns with no later Join "quietly evaporates", which is in effect a detached thread. The paper says nothing about what happens to other threads when the forking thread exits.

front: Detach: lecture says detaching lets the parent exit early. What do POSIX sources say detach does, and when do other threads outlive main?
back: Detach only lets a thread's storage be reclaimed without a join. Other threads outlive main only if it calls pthread_exit instead of returning.

front: Compiling PThreads: what header must be included, and what happens without it?
back: You must include pthread.h in the file containing pthreads code. Without it, the program will not compile.

front: Compiling PThreads: what flag links the pthreads library, and what is the better alternative on some platforms?
back: Pass -lpthread at compile time. On certain platforms -pthread is better: it links the pthreads library and configures the compilation for threads.

front: Compiling PThreads: what happens if you do not link the pthreads library?
back: The program may not report certain compilation errors at compile time, but it will still fail.

front: Compiling PThreads: what checking practice is recommended, especially for multithreaded programs?
back: Check the return values of common functions, such as those that create threads, create variables, or initialize data structures.

front: PThread Creation Example 1: what is passed as the second and fourth arguments to pthread_create, and why?
back: Both are NULL. The fourth is NULL because the start routine hello takes no arguments; the second is NULL because no custom attribute behavior is needed. After creating the threads, they must all be joined back in.

front: PThread Creation Example 1 (quiz 1): what does the program that creates four threads running hello print?
back: Hello Thread is printed four times, once by each created thread.

front: PThread Creation Example 2: what is passed as the final argument to pthread_create, and how does threadFunc use it?
back: The final argument is a pointer to the current value of the loop counter i. In threadFunc the pointer is cast to an integer pointer, then a local variable is assigned the value it points to, and that value is printed.

front: PThread Creation Example 2: what is the scope of p and myNum across the four threads?
back: Both are private to each thread. They exist only within the thread function's scope, so each of the four threads gets its own copies, which will likely hold different values.

front: PThread Creation Example 2: can the four threads print in a different order than they were created? Why?
back: Yes. We do not control how the threads are scheduled, so the order each reaches its printf can differ from creation order (e.g. 0, 2, 1, 3). Sequential output is also possible, and so is a third output with Thread Number 2 printed twice and no Thread Number 1 (explained in Example 3).

front: PThread Creation Example 3: the counter i is local to main, so how can the threads see its value change?
back: Because pthread_create is passed the address of i rather than a copy of its value. When main changes i, every thread reading through that address sees the new value. (The lecture calls i a "globally visible variable defined in main"; strictly it is local to main.)

front: PThread Creation Example 3: walk through how the second thread can read myNum == 2 when it was created at i == 1.
back: The second thread is created when i == 1, so ideally p points at i and myNum becomes 1. But before the thread casts the pointer and reads it, main may enter the next loop iteration and increment i to 2. Since the address of i was passed, p still points at i, so myNum takes the new value 2.

front: PThread Creation Example 3: how is the data race fixed with a tNum array?
back: Initialize an array tNum with one element per thread. On each loop iteration set tNum[i] = i, then pass the address of tNum[i] to pthread_create. Each thread reads its own private storage that is never modified, so incrementing i does not change the value a thread needs to see.

front: PThread Creation Example 3 (quiz 3): after the tNum fix, what outputs are possible?
back: Thread Number 0, 1, 2 and 3 each appear in the output, in any order: every thread now has private storage for its argument, but the scheduling order is still not controlled.

front: PThreads: what type represents a mutex?
back: pthread_mutex_t.

front: PThread mutexes: how does locking differ from Birrell's block construct?
back: Birrell protected a critical section with a block: the opening curly bracket meant the mutex was locked, the closing one meant it was released. In pthreads there is no implicit unlock; both lock and unlock must be called explicitly.

front: PThreads: give the signatures of the mutex lock and unlock calls, and what the region between them is.
back: int pthread_mutex_lock(pthread_mutex_t *mutex); and int pthread_mutex_unlock(pthread_mutex_t *mutex); Whatever code appears between them is the critical section.

front: PThreads: how does safe_insert look when rewritten from Birrell's block construct into pthreads?
back: It becomes an explicit pthread_mutex_lock, the insert into the shared list my_list, then an explicit pthread_mutex_unlock.

front: PThread mutexes: must a mutex be initialized before use, and what are the two ways shown in the lecture?
back: Yes, mutexes must be explicitly initialized: either call pthread_mutex_init or use the static initializer at declaration time.

front: PThreads: give the signature of pthread_mutex_init and what its attr argument controls.
back: int pthread_mutex_init(pthread_mutex_t *mutex, const pthread_mutexattr_t *attr); The attr argument specifies the mutex's behavior; passing NULL gives default behavior.

front: PThread mutexes: what is the default process-sharing behavior, and how can it change?
back: By default a mutex is private to a process, visible only to that process's threads. This can be changed explicitly so the mutex is shared with other processes.

front: PThreads: how does pthread_mutex_trylock differ from pthread_mutex_lock?
back: pthread_mutex_lock blocks the calling thread until it acquires the mutex. pthread_mutex_trylock acquires the mutex if it is free; if it is in use, it returns immediately, notifying the caller that the mutex is not available, so the thread is not blocked and can do something else and check again later.

front: PThreads: what call frees a mutex?
back: int pthread_mutex_destroy(pthread_mutex_t *mutex);

front: Mutex safety tips: what does "mutex scope must be global" mean?
back: The mutex must be visible to all threads; it cannot be private to a single thread, including main.

front: Mutex scope: lecture says a mutex's scope must be global. How does Birrell frame mutexes, and what do POSIX/OSTEP say the real requirement is?
back: Birrell says mutexes are ordinary data values, so a module managing many objects can protect each with its own mutex (e.g. one lock per open file plus one for the global table), allowing more parallelism. POSIX and OSTEP agree the requirement is only that every thread using the mutex can reach the same instance, not that it is a global variable.

front: PThreads: what type represents a condition variable?
back: pthread_cond_t.

front: PThreads: give the signature of pthread_cond_wait and describe what it does on entry and on wake-up.
back: int pthread_cond_wait(pthread_cond_t *cond, pthread_mutex_t *mutex); On entry it automatically releases the mutex and places the thread on the condition variable's wait queue. On wake-up it automatically reacquires the mutex before returning.

front: PThreads: give the signatures of pthread_cond_signal and pthread_cond_broadcast.
back: int pthread_cond_signal(pthread_cond_t *cond); and int pthread_cond_broadcast(pthread_cond_t *cond); Neither takes a mutex.

front: PThreads vs Birrell: which pthreads calls correspond to Birrell's Condition operations, and do the semantics differ?
back:
• Wait: pthread_cond_wait, which like Wait takes a condition variable and a mutex
  • Signal: pthread_cond_signal
  • Broadcast: pthread_cond_broadcast
The semantics are identical to Birrell's.

front: PThreads: give the signatures to create and destroy a condition variable.
back: int pthread_cond_init(pthread_cond_t *cond, const pthread_condattr_t *attr); and int pthread_cond_destroy(pthread_cond_t *cond);

front: PThreads: what does the condition variable attribute passed to pthread_cond_init control, and what is the default?
back: It controls whether the condition variable is used only by threads of a single process or is shared across processes. Passing NULL gives the default: private to a process.

front: Producer/consumer global state: what do buffer, add, rem, num, and BUF_SIZE represent?
back: buffer is the shared buffer; add and rem are the indices to add and remove elements; num is the number of elements in the queue; BUF_SIZE is 3 in this example.

front: Producer/consumer global state: what does an addition do, what does a removal do, and what are num, add, rem after two additions and one removal?
back: An addition writes at add, advances add, and increments num; a removal reads at rem, advances rem, and decrements num. All start at zero, so after two additions and one removal num is 1, add is 2, and rem is 1.

front: Producer/consumer global state: what synchronization variables are used, and how is the mutex initialized?
back: A mutex m and two condition variables c_cons and c_prod. The mutex is set up with the static initializer at declaration time rather than with a call to pthread_mutex_init.

front: Producer/consumer main: which functions do the two threads run, and what must main do before returning?
back: The first thread runs producer, the second runs consumer. They use default (non-detachable) behavior, so main must pthread_join them before returning. Neither function takes input, so NULL is passed as the argument; main checks each pthread_create return code to help debugging, then simply waits for both threads.

front: Producer/consumer producer: how many iterations does it loop, and what is its sequence after acquiring m?
back: It loops twenty times. After acquiring m with pthread_mutex_lock, it waits on c_prod with pthread_cond_wait if the buffer is full (num == BUF_SIZE). Once there is room (immediately, or after being woken), it adds its element and updates add and num.

front: Producer/consumer producer: why is m passed to pthread_cond_wait?
back: So the pthreads library knows which mutex to release while the thread waits and to reacquire afterwards.

front: Producer/consumer: how is the add/remove index advanced so it does not run off the end of the fixed buffer?
back: With modular arithmetic: add = (add + 1) % BUF_SIZE on the producer side and rem = (rem + 1) % BUF_SIZE on the consumer side, which wraps the index back to the front of the buffer.

front: Producer/consumer producer: after unlocking, which condition variable does it signal, and why signal rather than broadcast?
back: After unlocking the mutex it signals c_cons with pthread_cond_signal to tell consumers there is data. It signals rather than broadcasts because it inserted a single element, so only one consumer can proceed.

front: Producer/consumer consumer: how long does it loop, and what is its sequence after acquiring m?
back: It loops forever, continuously trying to remove elements. After acquiring m with pthread_mutex_lock, it waits on c_cons with pthread_cond_wait if the buffer is empty (num == 0). Once there is data (immediately, or after being woken), it removes an element and updates rem and num.

front: Producer/consumer: what sanity checks do the producer and consumer do after acquiring m?
back:
• Producer: overflow check, exits if num > BUF_SIZE
  • Consumer: underflow check, exits if num < 0

front: Producer/consumer consumer: on returning from pthread_cond_wait, what does it check, and what does it not assume?
back: It re-verifies that num is non-zero; it does not assume a producer actually left something in the buffer.

front: Producer/consumer consumer: why is it safe to signal c_prod after releasing the mutex?
back: It signals c_prod with pthread_cond_signal after unlocking the mutex, to tell the producer there is space. That is safe because the signal is unconditional at that point: it does not depend on the value of any shared variable.

front: Producer/consumer consumer: why does it signal c_prod rather than broadcast?
back: Consuming one element frees exactly one slot, so only one producer can proceed.
